title: Variables, Declarations and Initialization
learningObjectives: Explain the central rules behind variables, declarations and initialization in C.
Identify the relevant types, declarations, operators or library facilities.
Trace a worked example and explain its result.
Recognize common mistakes, portability concerns and unsafe assumptions.
Apply the concept in a small program and test normal and boundary cases.

understand.concept: A variable is an object with a type, a name, a storage duration and a lifetime. A declaration introduces an identifier and describes its type; a definition may also reserve storage. Initialization supplies an initial value when an object is created. C does not automatically initialize every local automatic object, so reading an uninitialized value can produce undefined behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: Types determine which values an object can represent and which operations are valid. Choose a type that matches the domain and initialize objects before reading them.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
A variable is an object with a type, a name, a storage duration and a lifetime. A declaration introduces an identifier and describes its type; a definition may also reserve storage. Initialization supplies an initial value when an object is created. C does not automatically initialize every local automatic object, so reading an uninitialized value can produce undefined behaviour.

Types determine which values an object can represent and which operations are valid. Choose a type that matches the domain and initialize objects before reading them.

When reviewing code, identify the declared types first, then trace conversions and the exact expression being evaluated. Compile with warnings enabled and test boundary values. Do not rely on assumptions about another compiler or machine.

practise.guidedTask: Create a program with variables for product count, unit price and subtotal. Initialize every object, calculate the subtotal and print it with matching format specifiers.
practise.independentTask: Model a small order with quantity, price, tax rate and final amount. Choose appropriate types, document units and test zero, negative and boundary inputs.
hints: Do not read an uninitialized automatic object.
A declaration and an initialization are related but not identical.
Use descriptive names and consistent units.
Select a type based on range and required precision.
Enable warnings and inspect conversion diagnostics.

questions.prompt: What is the safest general practice?
options: Choose types and operations deliberately, initialize data and validate assumptions.
Ignore warnings and assume values are valid.
Use casts to silence every warning.
questions.answer: Choose types and operations deliberately, initialize data and validate assumptions.
questions.explanation: Deliberate types and checks improve correctness.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a result is unexpected?
options: Create a small test case and inspect types, values and conversions.
Guess the result from the variable name.
questions.answer: Create a small test case and inspect types, values and conversions.
questions.explanation: Small reproducible tests make behaviour easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: Which statement about portability is accurate?
options: Some type sizes and ranges depend on the implementation.
All C implementations use identical type widths.
Compiler warnings change the C standard.
questions.answer: Some type sizes and ranges depend on the implementation.
questions.explanation: Use standard guarantees and inspect implementation limits.
